title: Emma Lazarus helped Jewish refugees and wrote the poem inscribed on the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty

trailer.text: Emma Lazarus, a Jewish writer and activist born in New York, was, according to the Jewish Women's Archive, an internationally known poet and writer.
In 1881 and 1882, when Jewish refugees streamed into New York Harbor, she dedicated herself to aiding them.
She visited them on Ward’s Island, taught them English and co-founded the Hebrew Technical Institute.
In 1883 she wrote “The New Colossus” to raise money for the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty.
In 1903, words from the poem were inscribed on a plaque placed inside the statue's pedestal.

stations.title: A girl in a wealthy New York home

paragraphs.text: Emma Lazarus was born on July 22, 1849, in New York, according to the National Park Service.
Her family was a wealthy sugar refining family of Portuguese Sephardic Jewish descent.
She was the fourth of Esther and Moses Lazarus’s seven children.
According to JTA, some of her ancestors were among the 23 Sephardic Jews who arrived in New York on September 13, 1654.
Her father, a successful sugar merchant, supported her writing and published her first book.
According to JTA, she grew up secular and was not especially attuned to Jewish communal issues.
According to the Poetry Foundation, reading George Eliot’s novel “Daniel Deronda” stirred her to consider her own heritage.
In the summer of 1877, a rise of genteel antisemitism in New York and its environs undermined her illusions about the acceptance of Jews in America.
The pogroms in Russia in the early 80s of the 19th century were a turning point in her identity as a poet and in her personal life.
In 1881 and 1882, Jewish refugees streamed into New York Harbor, and she dedicated herself to aiding them.
She visited the refugees at the Schiff Refuge on Ward’s Island and taught them English at the YMHA.
On Ward's Island she aided Jewish immigrants who had been detained by Castle Garden immigration officials.
While working there, she joked and quoted the question of what her society friends would say if they saw her there.
On October 14, 1882, rioting broke out among the Jewish immigrants on Ward's Island, who were arriving from Russia at the rate of about 2,000 per month.
According to historian Derek Penslar, the riot badly shook her.
The plight of the Russian Jews she met there deeply moved her, and these experiences influenced her writing.
Of the situation of the Russian refugees in New York, she said that the time had come for actions rather than words.

stations.title: A fund, an institute and letters

paragraphs.text: She started her own fund to help the refugees settle and find jobs.
She volunteered at the Hebrew Emigrant Aid Society.
She helped establish the Hebrew Technical Institute in New York, to provide vocational training for destitute Jewish immigrants.
In a series of fifteen open letters, from November 1882 to February 1883, she called on assimilated American Jews to support the refugees from Eastern Europe generously.
Her weekly column urged established American Jews to embrace the refugees.
According to the American Jewish Archives, she founded the Society for the Improvement and Colonization of East European Jews.
In England and France she met Jewish leaders to raise money for the new organization.
According to Esther Schor, in 1882 Lazarus was the first well-known American to publicly make the case for a Jewish state.
According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, she was an early advocate of a Jewish homeland in Palestine.
The citizens of France gave the statue to the citizens of the United States, in commemoration of both countries' commitment to liberty.
According to JTA, the poem was commissioned as part of a fundraiser for building the statue's pedestal.
In 1883, William Maxwell Evarts and author Constance Cary Harrison asked Lazarus to write a sonnet for an auction to benefit the pedestal.
It was an art and literary auction, run by the American Committee for the Statue of Liberty.
According to Wikipedia, Lazarus initially refused, and Harrison convinced her that the statue would be of great significance to immigrants sailing into the harbor.
According to a University of Houston digital library, when it was suggested that she write about the statue in the context of her beloved Jewish immigrants, she agreed to try.
According to the Poetry Foundation, she wrote a sonnet commemorating the plight of immigrants.
Thus “The New Colossus” was written in 1883.
After the auction, the sonnet appeared in Joseph Pulitzer's New York World as well as The New York Times.
According to Wikipedia, the exhibit closed after the pedestal was fully funded in August 1885.

stations.title: Forgotten, then a plaque in the pedestal

paragraphs.text: After its initial popularity, the sonnet slowly faded from public memory.
At the dedication of the statue in 1886, the poem was neither read nor mentioned.
In September 1887, Lazarus returned to New York gravely ill.
She died in New York on November 19, 1887, most likely from Hodgkin's lymphoma.
She was buried at Beth Olam Cemetery in Cypress Hills.
In 1901, approximately 14 years after her death, her friend Georgina Schuyler found a book containing the sonnet in a bookshop.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, Schuyler undertook to place a plaque with the poem inside the pedestal of the statue.
According to the University of Houston, the placement took two years of red tape and was completed thanks to the persistence of Schuyler and Gilder.
In 1903, words from the sonnet were inscribed on a plaque placed on the inner wall of the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty.
According to Wikipedia, the plaque was mounted on the pedestal's lower level.
According to the U.S. National Park Service, the 1903 plaque in the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty is made of bronze.

stations.title: The poem comes back to life

paragraphs.text: Only in the 1930s, in an age of restrictive immigration quotas, was “The New Colossus” brought back into circulation for the pro-immigration cause.
According to John Cunningham, it was the poem that permanently stamped on the Statue of Liberty the role of unofficial greeter of incoming immigrants.
Irving Berlin's 1949 musical “Miss Liberty” includes, as its final song, an adaptation of the last part of the poem.
On October 5, 1955, a plaque honoring Lazarus was unveiled at Battery Park.
On New York's Lower East Side, a high school named for her is tailored to English language learners.
In 2020, the American Jewish Historical Society in New York produced the “New Colossus” Project, with exhibitions, videos and a curriculum.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, in her time Lazarus was read by more American readers than any other Jewish writer of her century.
According to the same archive, she created the role of the American Jewish writer.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, both traditionalist Jews and Reform Jews ridiculed her for her Zionism.

According to The Jewish Press, her enthusiastic support for the return of Jews to the Land of Israel earned her enmity from two directions: from Reform Jews, who accused her of dual national loyalty, and from right-wing Orthodox Jews, who were sharply critical of her secular patriotism.
According to the same newspaper, even as she embraced her Judaism, she remained a bitter critic of Orthodox practice and Orthodox Jews.
According to the American Jewish Archives, the organization she founded for East European Jews collapsed the year after it was established.
Among all her eulogists, only Philip Cowen, editor of the American Hebrew, mentioned her Zionism.
Her sisters ignored her clear instructions and published her Jewish-themed poems and her translations in a separate second volume.
Her sister Annie Lazarus Johnston, who converted to Christianity, wrote that there was a tendency among the public to overemphasize the Hebraic side of her work, and that she greatly regretted it.
In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Ken Cuccinelli changed a line from the poem to support the public charge rule.

disagreements.question: When, and at what age, was her first book published?

versions.says: Jewish Women's Archive: her father published her first book when she was seventeen
JTA: her father privately published her first book of poems when she was 16
According to the American Jewish Archives, her father recognized her talent and himself published her first book, "Poems and Translations Written Between the Ages of Fourteen and Seventeen".

disagreements.question: Which generation of American Jews was she?

versions.says: Jewish Currents: the fourth generation of established American Jews
National Park Service: at Congregation Shearith Israel's Beth Olom Cemetery in Cypress Hills, Queens
JTA: at Beth Olam Cemetery in Cypress Hills, Brooklyn

disagreements.question: When was her organization founded, and when did she travel to raise money for it?

versions.says: American Jewish Archives: she founded the Society in 1883

On her first trip to Europe, in 1883, she met Jewish leaders in England and France to raise money for her new aid organization for refugees from Eastern Europe, the Society for the Colonisation and Improvement of Eastern European Refugees.

claims.text: לוחית לכבוד לזרוס נחשפה בפארק בטרי ב-5 באוקטובר 1955.
claims.quote: A plaque honoring Lazarus was unveiled at Battery Park on Oct. 5, 1955

claims.text: ב-2020 הפיקה החברה ההיסטורית היהודית האמריקנית בניו יורק פרויקט 'הקולוסוס החדש' של תערוכות, סרטונים ותוכנית לימוד.
claims.quote: In 2020, the American Jewish Historical Society in New York City produced a New Colossus Project of exhibitions, videos, and curriculum related to the poem.

claims.text: בימיה נקראה לזרוס יותר מכל סופר יהודי אחר במאה שלה, לפי ארכיון הנשים היהודיות.
claims.quote: Lazarus was read by more American readers than any other Jewish writer of her century.

claims.text: על הציונות שלה לגלגו עליה יהודים מסורתיים ויהודים רפורמים כאחד, לפי ארכיון הנשים היהודיות.
claims.quote: For her Zionism, she was ridiculed both by traditionalist Jews, who were put off by her secular patriotism, and by Reform Jews, who feared charges of dual nationality.

claims.text: לפי ה-Jewish Press, תמיכתה בשיבת יהודים לארץ ישראל זיכתה אותה בעוינות של יהודים רפורמים ושל אורתודוקסים.
claims.quote: earned her the enmity of both Reform Jews, who accused her of dual nationality, and right-wing Orthodox Jews, who were keenly critical of her secular patriotism

claims.text: לפי ה-Jewish Press, גם כשאימצה את יהדותה נותרה לזרוס מבקרת חריפה של הפרקטיקה האורתודוקסית ושל יהודים אורתודוקסים.
claims.quote: she remained a bitter critic of Orthodox practice and Orthodox Jews

claims.text: מבין כל המספידים, רק עורך 'אמריקן הברו' פיליפ קואן הזכיר את הציונות שלה.
claims.quote: Among all her eulogists, only Philip Cowen, editor of the American Hebrew, mentioned her Zionism.

claims.text: אחיותיה של לזרוס התעלמו מהוראותיה הברורות ופרסמו את שיריה בעלי הנושא היהודי ואת תרגומיה בכרך שני נפרד.
claims.quote: Lazarus’s sisters ignored her clear instructions, segregating her Jewish-themed poems and translations in a second volume.

claims.text: אחותה אנה לזרוס ג'ונסטון, שהתנצרה, כתבה שיש נטייה בציבור להגזים בצד העברי ביצירתה, דבר שהיא מצטערת עליו מאוד.
claims.quote: There has been a tendency on the part of the public to over emphasize the Hebraic strain of her work

claims.text: ב-2019, בממשל טראמפ הראשון, קן קוצ'ינלי שינה שורה מהשיר כדי לתמוך בכלל 'הנטל הציבורי'.
claims.quote: In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Ken Cuccinelli, whom Trump appointed as acting director of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, revised a line from the poem

claims.text: לפי JTA, ספר שיריה הראשון פורסם באופן פרטי בידי אביה כשהייתה בת 16.
claims.quote: first book of poems was privately published by her father when she was 16

claims.text: לפי ארכיון היהודים האמריקני, אביה פרסם בעצמו את ספרה הראשון ב-1886.
claims.quote: self-published her first book in 1886, which was titled Poems and Translations Written Between the Ages of Fourteen and Seventeen

claims.text: לפי שירות הפארקים הלאומיים של ארה"ב, הלוחית משנת 1903 שבבסיס פסל החירות עשויה מארד.
claims.quote: The 1903 bronze plaque located in the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty.
